APP: pulse-relay
CURRENT PHASE: design_handoff
PHASE PURPOSE: Produce a complete design handoff: screen-by-screen specs, interaction states, motion notes, design tokens, accessibility expectations, and a professional Claude Design prompt or import plan if the run is configured to pause for external design.

===== ORIGINAL PROMPT (initial_prompt.md) =====
Design and build a complex, production-shaped native iOS app that requires a
real server-side backend (not local-only, not a static/offline app) — pick a
genuinely creative, non-obvious idea that solves a real, specific pain point
well enough that it has a real shot at organic/viral growth. Do not default
to another todo-list, habit-tracker, journaling, or AI-wrapper app — those
categories are saturated and none of them are "unique." Think harder for an
underserved, emotionally sticky, inherently-social-or-real-time problem
where a mobile client + backend architecture is actually necessary (real-time
sync across users/devices, a shared/live data feed, matching or coordination
between people, server-side processing too heavy for on-device, etc.) — the
backend requirement should come from the idea being genuinely multi-user or
real-time, not be bolted on.

Requirements for the idea itself (spend real effort on this — the idea is
the deliverable, not just the code):
- Solves one specific, sharply-defined pain point for a specific audience
  (not "everyone"). Be able to state the pain point and audience in one
  sentence each.
- Has a natural viral/sharing loop baked into the core mechanic — not a
  bolted-on "invite friends" button, but something where using the app is
  inherently more valuable or fun with other people, or naturally produces
  something worth sharing outside the app.
- Genuinely requires a backend: real-time multiplayer/sync, a live shared
  feed, server-side matching/aggregation, push notifications driven by
  server-side events, or similar — justify the architecture choice.
- Is creative enough that a stranger hearing the one-line pitch would say
  "oh that's clever" rather than "isn't that just [existing app]?"

Technical scope:
- Native iOS client (SwiftUI).
- A real backend service (your choice of stack — pick something sensible
  and justify it) handling auth, data sync/storage, and whatever real-time
  or server-side logic the concept needs.
- Design the API contract, data model, and sync/real-time strategy properly
  before building — this is a "complicated app," not an MVP toy.
- Production-shaped: reasonable auth flow, error handling, loading/empty/
  offline states, and a coherent onboarding funnel a real user could follow.
- Visual design should be distinctive and match the concept — not generic
  default SwiftUI styling — but the primary bar for this app is the idea,
  the architecture, and it actually working end-to-end (client <-> backend).

Start by proposing and committing to the specific concept (pain point,
audience, viral loop, and why it needs a backend) before moving into specs
and build, and carry that concept consistently through naming, design, and
onboarding copy.

## Final Output

This phase confirms: **single-app build, no portfolio split.** The prompt asked for one native iOS app, and the concept that emerged from prompt_contract and product_research — a trust-graph-restricted, real-time pickup-relay coordination app for a school pickup pod — is inherently one app, not a decomposable set of sibling apps.

Selected app:
- **slug:** `pulse-relay`
- **category:** real-time trust-graph coordination / social-utility (explicitly not marketplace, not generic messaging, not "matching")
- **promise:** When a parent can't make pickup, their pod knows within seconds and exactly one person locks it in — no double coverage, no guessing who saw the message.
- **target user:** A parent/guardian of a child under 13 in a specific, pre-existing school-pickup pod (one classroom/carpool cluster) hit by an unplanned same-day pickup conflict.
- **build:** true

Rejected alternatives: splitting into sibling apps (separate requester/helper apps, a pod-admin companion app, a group-chat clone, a caregiver marketplace, a generic emergency-alert app); generic todo/habit/journal/AI-wrapper reskins; single-user-only designs; open stranger/proximity matching; daycare/activity pod variants in v1; location-tracking-first designs. `portfolio_json` is null — this is not a portfolio parent.

Build-priority guidance carried into later phases: if build time is constrained, cut breadth in secondary screens (pod management, profile/settings polish) before ever compromising the correctness or speed of the two locked core funnels (post relay request → pod visibility; accept → conflict-resolve → complete), since the core loop's trustworthiness is the entire value proposition.

{"phase": "initial_discussion", "one_paragraph_summary": "The initial_discussion phase locked a single, mutually-confirmed product definition for pulse-relay across two rounds. Product promise: a parent in a school-pickup pod broadcasts a same-day pickup coverage need and exactly one trusted pod member locks it in via a server-arbitrated first-accept-wins mechanism, with no ambiguity and no silent failure states. Primary user: a parent/guardian of a child under 13 in a specific, pre-existing school-pickup pod, acting one-handed under real time pressure with roughly ninety seconds of attention. The core loop was locked with explicit named states end-to-end: post request (no child PII) -> live pod visibility + push deep-link -> accept -> server-arbitrated first-accept-wins -> confirmed/already-covered states -> optional release/reopen -> optional time-aware still-open escalation with re-broadcast -> complete -> combined audit/receipt record. Two failure-mode requirements were elevated to core-loop, non-secondary status: acceptance is reversible until handoff completion, with an explicit release action that reopens the request and re-notifies the pod (~30s target), because an unretractable 'confirmed' state manufactures dangerous false certainty; and an unfulfilled request must show a visible, time-aware 'still open' state (not silence or a static pending label), because silent ambiguity on an actually-open request is an equally dangerous failure mode. The data model was required to support multiple simultaneously-open requests per pod (not a single-active-request assumption), even if the UI leads with a focused single card. ===== DECISIONS LOG (structured, authoritative) =====
- [DEC-prompt_contract-001] The deliverable is a single native SwiftUI iOS app with a real backend — no portfolio/multi-app interpretation.
  rationale: Prompt uses singular 'app' throughout with no quantity language.
  rejected: Building multiple small concept apps to hedge risk
  constraints: Later phases must not split scope into multiple unrelated apps
- [DEC-prompt_contract-002] Todo lists, habit trackers, journaling apps, and AI-wrapper apps are banned as the core offering, including disguised reskins of them.
  rationale: Explicitly forbidden in the prompt; reskins would violate the spirit even if not the letter.
  rejected: Allowing a reskinned habit tracker with social features bolted on
  constraints: A candidate concept must be checked against this list before being accepted
- [DEC-prompt_contract-003] Production-readiness is defined by checkable behaviors, not aesthetics: real empty/loading/error states verified under airplane mode and on a fresh zero-state account, session persistence across force-quit, and no UI claiming Saved/Synced/Sent without real backend acknowledgment.
  rationale: Prevents 'production-shaped' from being quietly redefined down to 'compiles and has a login screen'; matches this factory's recorded history of placeholder/blank-screen failures.
  rejected: Treating production-readiness as a subjective/aesthetic judgment call
  constraints: Every stateful screen must expose all four states before any later phase can claim it done
- [DEC-prompt_contract-004] The backend requirement must be provably load-bearing: the core value must fail or degrade for a solo user on one device with no second account/device involved.
  rationale: Prevents a bolted-on Firebase/API call from satisfying 'genuinely requires a backend' while the real experience is single-player.
  rejected: Accepting any app with a network call as satisfying the backend requirement
  constraints: Verification must include a live two-account/two-device test, not just an API existing
- [DEC-prompt_contract-005] The care-and-handoff relay concept for parents/guardians is carried forward as the working concept, provisionally, not as an immutable lock — it proceeds subject to a rollback gate if it fails the two-device/backend-load-bearing test or the safety constraints below.
  rationale: Resolves the round-1 phase-boundary disagreement: Codex wanted to commit now, Claude wanted concept-commitment treated as a distinct later step; both agreed a provisional-but-testable commitment satisfies both concerns.
  rejected: Treating the concept as fully and finally locked in this phase with no further challenge; Deferring all concept discussion to a separate phase with no candidate carried forward
  constraints: Any later phase must be able to reject or revise this concept if it fails the load-bearing backend test or safety constraints; Rollback must be explicit and documented if the concept is abandoned
- [DEC-prompt_contract-006] Matching is restricted to a pre-established trust graph (existing contacts, or verified members of a school/daycare pod a parent explicitly joins) — never open proximity-matching with unknown strangers.
  rationale: Removes the core safety liability of algorithmically pairing a child handoff with an unvetted stranger, while preserving every backend-necessity argument (live availability, real-time acceptance, capacity/routing logic).
  rejected: Open proximity-based matching with nearby unknown users; Leaving matching scope unspecified and deciding it ad hoc during build
  constraints: Data model and matching logic must enforce trust-graph/pod membership as a hard filter, not a ranking signal
- [DEC-prompt_contract-007] No UI element may imply identity verification, background-check completion, or safety vetting that the app does not actually perform; self-reported or peer-vouched trust must be labeled plainly as such.
  rationale: Prevents a decorative 'Verified' badge or trust score from being mistaken for real vetting in a context (child handoff) where that mistake is dangerous, not just misleading.
  rejected: Using unqualified 'Verified Guardian' badges based only on self-reported profile fields
  constraints: Design review and copy review must check every trust-related UI element against this rule before it ships
- [DEC-prompt_contract-008] Proof that a real backend endpoint is deployed and reachable from the iOS client is required as the first deliverable of the next (architecture/build) phase, before any concept-specific schema or screens are trusted as real.
  rationale: Both participants agreed 'genuinely requires a backend' is meaningless if reachability is never actually confirmed in this build environment; discovering this at final verification would be too late.
  rejected: Assuming backend reachability and confirming it only at final verification
  constraints: No feature-specific screen work should be considered validated until this reachability proof exists
- [DEC-prompt_contract-009] Naming and pitch framing must lead with the trust-graph/pod mechanic, not generic 'matching' language.
  rationale: Leading with 'matching' makes the pitch sound like derivative 'Uber for childcare,' which is both less clever and more alarming than the actual trust-graph-constrained mechanic.
  rejected: Pitching the app primarily around real-time matching/availability without foregrounding the pod/trust-graph structure
  constraints: Onboarding copy, app name, and marketing-style pitch language must foreground pod/trust-graph membership as the distinctive mechanic
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] The concept is framed as a micro-supply network for immediate care continuity among people who already know each other, not a marketplace, matching app, or social-discovery product.
  rationale: Keeps later phases from drifting toward marketplace/feed/discovery patterns that don't fit the trust-graph constraint from prompt_contract.
  rejected: Framing as a childcare marketplace or matching service

- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] The first build supports exactly one pod type: school pickup. Daycare and activity pod types are excluded from v1.
  rationale: Each additional pod type multiplies onboarding/verification surface (different join stories per context) before the core relay loop is even proven once; narrowing maximizes the chance of a fully-working, well-tested first version.

  rejected: Treating race-condition handling as an implementation detail left to the architecture/build phase without an explicit requirement or test case

- [DEC-initial_discussion-003] The core loop is: post request into pod (no child PII) -> live visibility + push notification deep-link -> accept -> server-arbitrated first-accept-wins -> explicit confirmed/already-covered states -> optional release/reopen -> optional still-open escalation -> complete -> combined audit/receipt record.
  rationale: Both participants converged on this exact sequence including the named states; it operationalizes the race-condition requirement from product_research into an actual UI flow.
  rejected: A simpler loop without explicit already-covered/reopened/still-open states
  constraints: Every named state (confirmed, already-covered, reopened, still-open, error) must be a distinct, visible UI state, not folded into a generic 'pending' or 'done' state
- [DEC-initial_discussion-004] Accepting a request is a reversible commitment until handoff is marked complete; releasing ("I can no longer cover this") is a first-class action that immediately reopens the request and re-notifies the pod, targeted at under ~30 seconds.
  rationale: An accept state with no way to back out manufactures false confidence for a parent under stress, which is a worse failure mode than the ambiguous group chat this app replaces.
  rejected: Treating acceptance as final/irreversible with no in-app release mechanism; Treating back-out as a nice-to-have deferred to v2
  constraints: This must be built as a core-loop requirement at the same priority as the accept race-condition test, not as secondary polish
- [DEC-initial_discussion-005] An unfulfilled request must show a visible, time-aware 'still open' state (e.g. elapsed time since posting) with a re-broadcast path, rather than a static pending indicator or silence.
  rationale: A false 'nothing is happening' read on an actually-open request is as dangerous as a false 'confirmed' read, because it hides the time-dependent information a stressed parent needs to decide whether to escalate outside the app.
  rejected: A generic static 'pending' or 'waiting' label with no elapsed-time signal; Leaving unfulfilled requests with no distinct visible state
  constraints: The request card must surface elapsed time, not just a binary open/closed status
- [DEC-initial_discussion-006] The data model must support multiple simultaneously-open requests per pod, each with independent identity (requester, urgency) and independently acceptable, even though the UI may optimize for a single focused card.

  rejected: Modeling single-active-request-per-pod as a hard constraint with multi-request support deferred to v2; Leaving concurrent-request behavior undefined and deciding it ad hoc during build
  constraints: API contract and data model in the next phase must not assume one open request per pod at any given time

  rejected: Building a full pod-admin console with member management and settings in v1
  constraints: Any pod-admin capability (removing a bad actor, editing pod settings) is explicitly deferred to v2, not built now

**Must-have features for pulse-relay v1**, split by execution priority (Tier-1 = the literal two-phone demo, cannot be rushed under any time pressure; Tier-2 = fully required but can ship with rougher finish before Tier-1 ever does):

*Tier-1 (demo-critical, several flagged uncuttable):*
- Auth with session persistence across force-quit
- Zero-dead-end onboarding: create or join a pod by invite code/link
- Post a same-day request with no child PII
- **[uncuttable]** Honest delivery-count copy ("Sent to N pod members") from real push-token status, with a weak-delivery warning
- **[uncuttable]** Server commits the CAS write and dispatches the APNs push within a strict server-owned bound (~2s happy-path target); actual device receipt is observed in the two-device demo, not a hard contractual number, since Apple's push infrastructure is best-effort
- **[uncuttable]** Server-side compare-and-swap accept arbitration — no polling or client-side arbitration
- **[uncuttable]** Deterministic resolution to exactly one confirmed winner and one explicit "already covered by [name]" loser, sourced from the CAS result
- **[uncuttable]** No optimistic UI anywhere — an explicit awaiting-confirmation state precedes every terminal state on post/accept/release/complete/withdraw
- **[uncuttable]** The literal two-device side-by-side demo itself: one device confirms, the other shows already-covered, within a second or two, zero chat, zero manual reconciliation

*Tier-2 (required, finish-quality flexible):*
- Release/reopen with pod re-notify (~30s target)
- Requester-only `withdrawn` terminal state, CAS-arbitrated, no audit/receipt artifact, mutually exclusive with `release` by state
- Still-open state with visible elapsed time and re-broadcast
- Completion produces one immutable audit/receipt object (internal + shareable privacy-filtered views)

*Also must, no tiering ambiguity:*
- Trust-graph/pod-membership enforcement on all reads/writes
- Multi-open-request data model with deterministic ordering
- Idempotent client action IDs + crash/relaunch reconciliation from server truth (named force-quit-mid-accept test)
- Server-side UTC + pod-home-timezone time math, no client-local-time logic
- Pod-creator join-code revoke/reissue
- Audit/receipt persists through account deletion (departed party shown as placeholder)
- "Accepted" copy states claimed-responsibility only, never guaranteed arrival
- Distinct empty states: pod-of-one vs. populated-but-unresponsive pod
- Four states (loading/empty/error/success) on both core funnels
- **One tokenized Theme.swift with zero literals elsewhere, full dark-mode coverage on every core screen — hard must, same weight as trust-graph enforcement, given two prior design-lint incidents on exactly this failure**
- Free tier includes the entire core loop (post/accept/release/complete/withdraw + receipt) forever for at least one pod; nothing safety-related gated behind payment
- Single native SwiftUI app, one Xcode project, no portfolio split

**Should/could:** deterministic active-request ordering, retry-with-backoff copy, subtle/reduced-motion-safe transition haptics, a lightweight onboarding helper card, a minimal profile/sign-out screen, the shareable receipt card's visual polish (explicitly subordinate to the already-covered transition), an inert unused entitlement schema field.

**Won't-build this phase:** child PII (name/photo/face), location/GPS/ETA/maps, in-app chat/DM, payments, recurring/scheduled requests, a persistent history/feed screen, any pod-admin console beyond create-code + revoke/reissue, moderation/report/mute/remove tooling, identity-verification or background-check badges, open stranger/proximity matching, and — locked explicitly this phase — any StoreKit/paywall implementation, multi-pod switching UI, or critical-alert entitlement build-out.

*Tier-1 (demo-critical, several flagged uncuttable):*
- Auth with session persistence across force-quit
- Zero-dead-end onboarding: create or join a pod by invite code/link
- Post a same-day request with no child PII
- **[uncuttable]** Honest delivery-count copy ("Sent to N pod members") from real push-token status, with a weak-delivery warning
- **[uncuttable]** Server commits the CAS write and dispatches the APNs push within a strict server-owned bound (~2s happy-path target); actual device receipt is observed in the two-device demo, not a hard contractual number, since Apple's push infrastructure is best-effort
- **[uncuttable]** Server-side compare-and-swap accept arbitration — no polling or client-side arbitration
- **[uncuttable]** Deterministic resolution to exactly one confirmed winner and one explicit "already covered by [name]" loser, sourced from the CAS result
- **[uncuttable]** No optimistic UI anywhere — an explicit awaiting-confirmation state precedes every terminal state on post/accept/release/complete/withdraw
- **[uncuttable]** The literal two-device side-by-side demo itself: one device confirms, the other shows already-covered, within a second or two, zero chat, zero manual reconciliation

*Tier-2 (required, finish-quality flexible):*
- Release/reopen with pod re-notify (~30s target)
- Requester-only `withdrawn` terminal state, CAS-arbitrated, no audit/receipt artifact, mutually exclusive with `release` by state
- Still-open state with visible elapsed time and re-broadcast
- Completion produces one immutable audit/receipt object (internal + shareable privacy-filtered views)

*Also must, no tiering ambiguity:*
- Trust-graph/pod-membership enforcement on all reads/writes
- Multi-open-request data model with deterministic ordering
- Idempotent client action IDs + crash/relaunch reconciliation from server truth (named force-quit-mid-accept test)
- Server-side UTC + pod-home-timezone time math, no client-local-time logic
- Pod-creator join-code revoke/reissue
- Audit/receipt persists through account deletion (departed party shown as placeholder)
- "Accepted" copy states claimed-responsibility only, never guaranteed arrival
- Distinct empty states: pod-of-one vs. populated-but-unresponsive pod
- Four states (loading/empty/error/success) on both core funnels
- **One tokenized Theme.swift with zero literals elsewhere, full dark-mode coverage on every core screen — hard must, same weight as trust-graph enforcement, given two prior design-lint incidents on exactly this failure**
- Free tier includes the entire core loop (post/accept/release/complete/withdraw + receipt) forever for at least one pod; nothing safety-related gated behind payment
- Single native SwiftUI app, one Xcode project, no portfolio split

**Should/could:** deterministic active-request ordering, retry-with-backoff copy, subtle/reduced-motion-safe transition haptics, a lightweight onboarding helper card, a minimal profile/sign-out screen, the shareable receipt card's visual polish (explicitly subordinate to the already-covered transition), an inert unused entitlement schema field.

The design should be deliberately named as “Signal Relay HUD” for a parent pickup pod, because the value is instantaneous, high-signal coordination, not productivity or sociality. The rationale is: this is a real-time safety-critical relay, so the interface should read like a calm dispatch panel where ambiguity is eliminated by explicit state, not like a feed where people infer intent from silence.

The emotional target is: when the user opens the app in a thirty-second panic window, they should feel one-step-in, low-friction, and never unsure whether a pickup is claimed, pending, or still unclaimed.

The signature interaction should be one central relay card that behaves like a live control surface: post a request, see a numeric elapsed timer immediately visible, and the “Cover this pickup” action transitions through a clear pending-to-confirmed path only after backend ack. In accepted or loser states, the card should visibly transform (not just text switch), so the user sees at that instant what happened to that exact request and who owns it next.

For the core screen language, I would reject a default SwiftUI version that uses plain NavigationStack + List + standard blue buttons + default typography as unsuitable. Three concrete differences are required: first, no default list chrome; requests are rendered as high-contrast cards with explicit state chips and large readable action zones; second, no default system typography/colors; every text size, spacing, and color comes from Theme.swift so dark mode is guaranteed semantic parity; third, the state transitions are visualized as deterministic timeline/status cards (e.g., Open → Awaiting Claim → Claimed by X / Already covered by X / Still open 02:14 / Withdrawn) instead of a single “Pending” label with no elapsed-time meaning.

I would define screen inventory as eight concrete screens/containers so the build is end-to-end and testable:

Screen-level states must be explicit to prevent blank screens and false certainty:

Launch/session should have loading (validating token), signed-out idle, auth-ing (Apple sign-in pending), authenticated, and error (expired token, network).

## Final Output

**Design language:** *Relay HUD* — an instrument-panel identity you trust under stress, not a chat feed you have to parse. "Beacon" lives on as the name of the signature motion (pulse-to-latch) and should show up in code as the literal component name (e.g. `BeaconCard`/`RelayBeaconView`), not as a second brand term.

**Palette (semantic, in Theme.swift only):** amber-pulse = open/live/awaiting; warm teal-green (not stoplight green) = confirmed/claimed; slate/muted gray = terminal non-actionable (withdrawn, complete); true red = reserved exclusively for genuine system/network errors, never for the accept-race loser or any other normal-outcome state.

**Signature interaction:** cards pulse on a calm heartbeat rhythm while awaiting server ack, then convert to a steady locked panel on resolution. The accept-race winner and loser get the *identical* fast, mechanical, half-second latch treatment — no shake, no alert icon, no red — so "already covered by [name]" reads as "worked as designed," not a malfunction, at a glance and without reading text. Reduce Motion collapses this to an instant but still visually distinct crossfade.

**Chrome rejected:** no default List/Form rows, no system-blue NavigationStack accents, no vanishing toast confirmations. Every outcome-affecting state is persistent and card-resident, sourced only from real backend acknowledgment.

**Screen scope (narrow, no added branching):** session/auth gate, pod onboarding (create/join with true empty states), live relay board, request composer, request detail (accept/release/withdraw), receipt, minimal profile/pod-settings.

**Secondary-screen constraints (operationalized, not vibes):** receipt/profile/pod-settings inherit Theme tokens, spacing, typography, and state language but get zero bespoke motion — no custom transitions beyond system default, no bespoke empty-state illustration (a plain SF Symbol + one line of Theme-styled text is enough), no color treatment outside the shared semantic palette. Carve-out: the receipt card gets a higher bar for typography/information-hierarchy quality since it leaves the app via the share sheet and represents the product to a non-user — but still no second signature animation.

**All-clear resting state (new, locked this round):** the live board's default "nothing's happening" state — what users see the vast majority of the time — is a real designed screen, not a blank view: pod name, member count, a quiet at-rest "all clear" indicator using the same slate/teal semantic language (present, not pulsing), and the post-request CTA as the obvious single action. No unique motion of its own; it just has to be genuinely composed content per the existing global empty-state rule.

**Craft-budget priority if time runs short:** (1) open→awaiting pulse, (2) deterministic winner/loser latch, (3) completed/withdrawn terminal card clarity. Everything else — secondary screens, resting state included — stays plain and correct rather than getting unique polish.

----- Testing And Quality -----
# Testing & Quality for a Small iOS App

Target: **iOS 17+ deployment / Swift 5.9+**, built with **Xcode 16 or later** (Swift Testing ships in-box; use `OS=latest` in CI so the simulator version tracks your toolchain). Zero third-party deps — everything here is Apple first-party. This is a pragmatic reference for an AI building a prototype: maximize confidence per line of test code, avoid brittle tests that break on every UI tweak.

---

## TL;DR strategy for a prototype

- **Don't chase coverage.** Test the code that would be embarrassing or expensive if wrong: money math, date logic, parsing, persistence round-trips, state machines, reducers/view models.
- **Skip testing SwiftUI view bodies.** Use **Xcode Previews** as your visual feedback loop instead — they are faster than any UI test.
- **Make logic testable by moving it out of views** into plain `struct`/`class` types with injected dependencies. If it's testable, it's usually also better architected.
- **One happy-path UI test** through the primary flow catches wiring/regression bugs that unit tests can't. More than a handful of UI tests is usually a net negative for a prototype (slow, flaky).
- **Prefer Swift Testing (`@Test`)** for new unit tests. Keep XCTest for **UI tests** (`XCUIApplication`) and **performance tests** (`measure`) — those APIs are XCTest-only.

Priority order to write tests, highest first:
1. Pure logic with branches (pricing, validation, formatting, sorting/filtering).
2. View model / reducer state transitions (given input → expected observable state).
3. Persistence & serialization round-trips (Codable, SwiftData/UserDefaults).
4. Networking mappers (raw JSON → domain model), with a fake session — never hit the real network.
5. One end-to-end UI smoke test of the core flow.

---

## Project setup

- **Unit test target**: File ▸ New ▸ Target ▸ *Unit Testing Bundle*. Choose **Swift Testing** (default in Xcode 16+) or XCTest.
- **UI test target**: separate *UI Testing Bundle* — it launches the app as a black box.
- Add app code to tests with `@testable import YourApp` (unit tests only; gives access to `internal` symbols). UI tests use the accessibility layer, not imports.
- A `.xctestplan` lets you group tests, set env vars, and pick run configurations (e.g. randomized order). One default plan is fine for a prototype.
- Swift Testing and XCTest **coexist in the same target and same run** — migrate incrementally.

---

## Swift Testing (`@Test`) — the modern default

Import `Testing`, not `XCTest`. Tests are global functions or methods annotated `@Test`; assertions use `#expect` (non-fatal, keeps going) and `#require` (fatal, unwraps/stops).

```swift
import Testing
@testable import MyApp

@Test func totalIncludesTax() {
    let cart = Cart(items: [.init(price: 10), .init(price: 5)])
    #expect(cart.total(taxRate: 0.1) == 16.5)
}
```

- `#expect(expr)` records a failure and **continues** — the macro captures sub-expression values, so a failure prints the actual operands (no need for XCTest-style messages).
- `#require(expr)` throws and **halts the test** on failure — use it for preconditions where continuing is pointless. It also unwraps optionals (call in a `throws` test with `try`):

```swift
@Test func parsesUser() throws {
    let user = try #require(User(json: validJSON))  // stops here if nil
    #expect(user.name == "Ada")
}
```

### Suites and shared setup

Group with a `struct` (preferred) or `final class`. A **fresh instance is created per test**, so `init` is your per-test setup — no shared mutable state between tests by default.

```swift
@Suite("Cart pricing")
struct CartTests {
    let cart: Cart              // built fresh for every @Test below

    init() { cart = Cart(items: [.init(price: 10)]) }

    @Test func emptyTaxIsIdentity() {
        #expect(cart.total(taxRate: 0) == 10)
    }
}
```

Teardown: for a `struct` suite there usually is none — value types just drop when the instance goes away. If you genuinely need cleanup, use a `final class` and put it in `deinit`. Note `deinit` **cannot be `async` or `throwing`** and can't be actor-isolated, so for `@MainActor` suites or async cleanup, do the work at the end of each test (or use a custom scoping trait) rather than relying on `deinit`.

### Parameterized tests — one test, many cases

Replaces copy-pasted test bodies. Each argument runs as a **separate, independently-reported case**. A single array of tuples destructures positionally into multiple parameters:

```swift
@Test(arguments: [
    ("", false),
    ("a@b.co", true),
    ("no-at", false),
])
func validatesEmail(_ input: String, _ expected: Bool) {
    #expect(EmailValidator.isValid(input) == expected)
}
```

Destructuring is positional — element labels in the tuples don't have to match parameter names and are best omitted to avoid confusion. Cross-product of two sequences (every combination):

```swift
@Test(arguments: [1, 2, 3], ["x", "y"])   // 6 cases
func combos(n: Int, s: String) { #expect(!s.isEmpty && n > 0) }
```

Wrap in `zip(a, b)` when you want **paired** (not cross-product) cases:

```swift
@Test(arguments: zip([1, 2, 3], ["a", "b", "c"]))   // 3 cases
func paired(n: Int, s: String) { #expect(n > 0 && !s.isEmpty) }
```

### Traits: naming, tagging, skipping, known bugs

```swift
@Test("Discount never goes negative")                       // display name
@Test(.disabled("flaky until CI fix"))                      // skip, stays visible
@Test(.enabled(if: FeatureFlags.checkoutV2))                // conditional run
@Test(.bug("https://example.com/issue/42", "rounding"))     // url first, then title
@Test(.tags(.fast))                                         // group across files
```

Define tags once (do **not** add `@Test` — a tag is not a test):

```swift
extension Tag { @Tag static var fast: Self }
```

Run a subset from the CLI with `swift test --filter` / `xcodebuild ... -only-testing:`, or filter by tag in Xcode's Test navigator.

===== DECISIONS LOG (structured, authoritative) =====
- [DEC-prompt_contract-001] The deliverable is a single native SwiftUI iOS app with a real backend — no portfolio/multi-app interpretation.
  rationale: Prompt uses singular 'app' throughout with no quantity language.
  rejected: Building multiple small concept apps to hedge risk
  constraints: Later phases must not split scope into multiple unrelated apps
- [DEC-prompt_contract-002] Todo lists, habit trackers, journaling apps, and AI-wrapper apps are banned as the core offering, including disguised reskins of them.
  rationale: Explicitly forbidden in the prompt; reskins would violate the spirit even if not the letter.
  rejected: Allowing a reskinned habit tracker with social features bolted on
  constraints: A candidate concept must be checked against this list before being accepted
- [DEC-prompt_contract-003] Production-readiness is defined by checkable behaviors, not aesthetics: real empty/loading/error states verified under airplane mode and on a fresh zero-state account, session persistence across force-quit, and no UI claiming Saved/Synced/Sent without real backend acknowledgment.
  rationale: Prevents 'production-shaped' from being quietly redefined down to 'compiles and has a login screen'; matches this factory's recorded history of placeholder/blank-screen failures.
  rejected: Treating production-readiness as a subjective/aesthetic judgment call
  constraints: Every stateful screen must expose all four states before any later phase can claim it done
- [DEC-prompt_contract-004] The backend requirement must be provably load-bearing: the core value must fail or degrade for a solo user on one device with no second account/device involved.
  rationale: Prevents a bolted-on Firebase/API call from satisfying 'genuinely requires a backend' while the real experience is single-player.
  rejected: Accepting any app with a network call as satisfying the backend requirement
  constraints: Verification must include a live two-account/two-device test, not just an API existing
- [DEC-prompt_contract-005] The care-and-handoff relay concept for parents/guardians is carried forward as the working concept, provisionally, not as an immutable lock — it proceeds subject to a rollback gate if it fails the two-device/backend-load-bearing test or the safety constraints below.
  rationale: Resolves the round-1 phase-boundary disagreement: Codex wanted to commit now, Claude wanted concept-commitment treated as a distinct later step; both agreed a provisional-but-testable commitment satisfies both concerns.
  rejected: Treating the concept as fully and finally locked in this phase with no further challenge; Deferring all concept discussion to a separate phase with no candidate carried forward
  constraints: Any later phase must be able to reject or revise this concept if it fails the load-bearing backend test or safety constraints; Rollback must be explicit and documented if the concept is abandoned
- [DEC-prompt_contract-006] Matching is restricted to a pre-established trust graph (existing contacts, or verified members of a school/daycare pod a parent explicitly joins) — never open proximity-matching with unknown strangers.
  rationale: Removes the core safety liability of algorithmically pairing a child handoff with an unvetted stranger, while preserving every backend-necessity argument (live availability, real-time acceptance, capacity/routing logic).
  rejected: Open proximity-based matching with nearby unknown users; Leaving matching scope unspecified and deciding it ad hoc during build
  constraints: Data model and matching logic must enforce trust-graph/pod membership as a hard filter, not a ranking signal
- [DEC-prompt_contract-007] No UI element may imply identity verification, background-check completion, or safety vetting that the app does not actually perform; self-reported or peer-vouched trust must be labeled plainly as such.
  rationale: Prevents a decorative 'Verified' badge or trust score from being mistaken for real vetting in a context (child handoff) where that mistake is dangerous, not just misleading.
  rejected: Using unqualified 'Verified Guardian' badges based only on self-reported profile fields
  constraints: Design review and copy review must check every trust-related UI element against this rule before it ships
- [DEC-prompt_contract-008] Proof that a real backend endpoint is deployed and reachable from the iOS client is required as the first deliverable of the next (architecture/build) phase, before any concept-specific schema or screens are trusted as real.
  rationale: Both participants agreed 'genuinely requires a backend' is meaningless if reachability is never actually confirmed in this build environment; discovering this at final verification would be too late.
  rejected: Assuming backend reachability and confirming it only at final verification
  constraints: No feature-specific screen work should be considered validated until this reachability proof exists
- [DEC-prompt_contract-009] Naming and pitch framing must lead with the trust-graph/pod mechanic, not generic 'matching' language.
  rationale: Leading with 'matching' makes the pitch sound like derivative 'Uber for childcare,' which is both less clever and more alarming than the actual trust-graph-constrained mechanic.
  rejected: Pitching the app primarily around real-time matching/availability without foregrounding the pod/trust-graph structure
  constraints: Onboarding copy, app name, and marketing-style pitch language must foreground pod/trust-graph membership as the distinctive mechanic
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] The concept is framed as a micro-supply network for immediate care continuity among people who already know each other, not a marketplace, matching app, or social-discovery product.
  rationale: Keeps later phases from drifting toward marketplace/feed/discovery patterns that don't fit the trust-graph constraint from prompt_contract.
  rejected: Framing as a childcare marketplace or matching service
  constraints: Naming, copy, and IA in later phases must reflect trust-transfer/coordination, not marketplace or social discovery
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] The first build supports exactly one pod type: school pickup. Daycare and activity pod types are excluded from v1.
  rationale: Each additional pod type multiplies onboarding/verification surface (different join stories per context) before the core relay loop is even proven once; narrowing maximizes the chance of a fully-working, well-tested first version.
  rejected: Supporting school, daycare, and activity pods in parallel from v1
  constraints: Data model's pod entity should not be built polymorphic for multiple pod types until school-pickup is proven; Later phases may propose additional pod types only as an explicit v2+ extension

  rejected: Requiring pre-existing pod membership with no in-app path to join or create one

  constraints: Every core-loop screen must be legible and actionable in a single glance under stress

  rationale: Both participants converged on this exact sequence including the named states; it operationalizes the race-condition requirement from product_research into an actual UI flow.
  rejected: A simpler loop without explicit already-covered/reopened/still-open states

  rejected: Treating acceptance as final/irreversible with no in-app release mechanism; Treating back-out as a nice-to-have deferred to v2
  constraints: This must be built as a core-loop requirement at the same priority as the accept race-condition test, not as secondary polish

  rejected: A generic static 'pending' or 'waiting' label with no elapsed-time signal; Leaving unfulfilled requests with no distinct visible state

## Phase Purpose

Decide UX flows, information architecture, key screens/states, and the design principles that govern them.

## Transcript


### Round 1


**Codex (Product Strategist · Pragmatist) — Round 1**

The design should be deliberately named as “Signal Relay HUD” for a parent pickup pod, because the value is instantaneous, high-signal coordination, not productivity or sociality. The rationale is: this is a real-time safety-critical relay, so the interface should read like a calm dispatch panel where ambiguity is eliminated by explicit state, not like a feed where people infer intent from silence.

The emotional target is: when the user opens the app in a thirty-second panic window, they should feel one-step-in, low-friction, and never unsure whether a pickup is claimed, pending, or still unclaimed.

The signature interaction should be one central relay card that behaves like a live control surface: post a request, see a numeric elapsed timer immediately visible, and the “Cover this pickup” action transitions through a clear pending-to-confirmed path only after backend ack. In accepted or loser states, the card should visibly transform (not just text switch), so the user sees at that instant what happened to that exact request and who owns it next.

For the core screen language, I would reject a default SwiftUI version that uses plain NavigationStack + List + standard blue buttons + default typography as unsuitable. Three concrete differences are required: first, no default list chrome; requests are rendered as high-contrast cards with explicit state chips and large readable action zones; second, no default system typography/colors; every text size, spacing, and color comes from Theme.swift so dark mode is guaranteed semantic parity; third, the state transitions are visualized as deterministic timeline/status cards (e.g., Open → Awaiting Claim → Claimed by X / Already covered by X / Still open 02:14 / Withdrawn) instead of a single “Pending” label with no elapsed-time meaning.

I would define screen inventory as eight concrete screens/containers so the build is end-to-end and testable:
Launch & session gate for sign-in persistence, Pod onboarding (create/join), Main relay board, Post request composer, Relay request detail/resolve, Release flow sheet, Withdraw flow, and Audit/receipt view, plus a minimal profile/sign-out fallback screen.

Primary flow should stay narrow and deterministic: (1) first-time user lands on session gate, signs in once; (2) zero-state onboarding branches to create or join pod by invite code/link; (3) authenticated pod member reaches relay board; if there are no members, they get a specific invite-empty state; if members exist but nothing happened, they get a “waiting” empty state with a re-broadcast CTA; (4) user taps New Relay, submits same-day request with short note, waits through awaiting-confirmation, sees honest “sent to N members” delivery copy; (5) request appears live with elapsed timer; (6) another member opens deep link, taps Cover, waits through awaiting-confirmation, both devices converge via CAS result; only one confirms and one shows already-covered-by-name; (7) requester can complete or release if claimed, or withdraw if unclaimed; (8) complete emits the immutable receipt/audit artifact with internal and shareable projection.

Screen-level states must be explicit to prevent blank screens and false certainty:

Launch/session should have loading (validating token), signed-out idle, auth-ing (Apple sign-in pending), authenticated, and error (expired token, network).  
Pod onboarding should have no-pod-empty, create in progress, join in progress, invalid/expired code error, created/joined success, and retryable network error; there is no silent trap path.  
Relay board should have loading, empty-with-no-other-members, empty-but-populated-no-response, success-with-active-requests, and error. The board should render multi-open requests independently but can foreground the most urgent/oldest for stress clarity.  
Post-request flow should have compose, awaiting-confirmation (tap-lock), posted-open-success, and post-failed states; no optimistic “posted” without server ack.  
Request detail/resolve should have loading, open-unclaimed, awaiting-accept, confirmed-by-me, already-covered-by-other, released-reopened, still-open-aged, withdrawn, completed, and error/retry states, with backend-tied outcomes only.  
Release sheet should have confirm intent, awaiting-confirmation, success-reopened, and failure with safe retry.  
Withdraw flow should have confirm withdrawal, awaiting-confirmation, withdrawn-success, and unavailable/forbidden when no longer applicable.  
Receipt view should have loading, loaded with full artifact, loaded-with-placeholder identities for deleted users, and export/share-ready state where share exists only as projection copy.

Navigation should be simple: one tabless root path or shallow stack with clear back actions; no chat room, no extra branching. Core navigation only needs “Create/Join Pod,” “Open Request,” “Resolve,” and “Receipt,” with an explicit close/exit path that never destroys state.

Accessibility requirements are non-negotiable: all copy must have explicit role labels in VoiceOver (“Request by requester, status open, elapsed two minutes, claim button”), haptic patterns should never be the only cue for success/failure, and every status change should include both color and text/icon. Use semantic colors and contrast-safe tokens, support Dynamic Type, avoid clipping/overlap through strict fixed minimum spacings from Theme.swift, keep interactive targets at or above comfortable touch size, include reduced-motion-safe transitions, and ensure state text remains legible under both appearances.

The biggest risk in this direction is overfitting to polish and drifting into extra surface area (profile/settings, request history, or a fancy feed) before the claim/no-claim ambiguity loop is perfect. The detail that must be preserved in the final spec is this: every terminal state shown to users (confirmed, already covered, withdrawn, complete, still open) must come from server truth and can only appear after explicit acknowledgment of an idempotent action, and the UI must always surface elapsed time for open requests instead of a vague pending state.

**Claude (Design Lead · User Advocate) — Round 1**

Coming at this fresh: the single biggest design risk I see is that this app is used rarely — most of the time a parent opens it, nothing is happening, the pod is quiet — and yet the one time something IS happening, it's genuinely stressful. That asymmetry should drive every visual decision. I want to name the design language "Relay Beacon" — a dispatch-radio aesthetic borrowed from volunteer fire-pager and CB-radio status lights: a request pulses like a beacon while open, and locks into a solid, steady light the instant someone claims it. The rationale isn't decorative — status-light color coding (amber pulsing = open/waiting, steady green = claimed, slate gray = withdrawn/complete) is something people read instantly under stress without having to parse words first, the same way you read a traffic light without thinking, and it literally embodies the product's name (Pulse / Relay) instead of being an arbitrary skin. This is not "clean and modern" — swap in any other app's name and this description stops making sense, because it's built around the specific mechanic of a signal passing hand-to-hand through a trusted group and locking shut the moment it's caught.

Emotional target for the main screen: the parent should feel the specific relief of watching a status light snap from blinking to solid — "it's handled, I can stop watching this" — not the low-grade dread of scrolling an unread group chat wondering if anyone saw your message.

Signature interaction: when a request posts, it pulses outward from the card like a heartbeat/radar ping while awaiting server confirmation. On ack, that pulse either locks into a solid confirmed state with the accepter's name sliding in like a bolt latching shut, or — if you were the second person to tap accept — the card performs that same calm latch animation but locks to "already covered by [name]." That losing transition is the one moment I'd protect above all others: it must not read as an error (no red, no shake, no exclamation icon), because the app working exactly as designed is what that screen represents, and it's already flagged uncuttable in the requirements. If it looks like a malfunction, the whole product concept collapses in a stranger's first impression.

The default version of this app — the one I'm explicitly rejecting — would be a plain SwiftUI List of request rows, system blue accents, default NavigationStack titles, and a generic green toast that flashes "Accepted!" and disappears. Three concrete things that must differ: first, no List/Form chrome for the live board — it's a small card stack, not scrollable rows, because a row-list reads as an inbox, which recreates the exact ambiguous-group-chat mental model this app exists to kill. Second, no system blue anywhere as a state color — every color on screen is drawn from the amber/green/slate status-light palette and means something specific, never decoration. Third, no transient toast/alert for outcome-affecting actions — confirmed, already-covered, withdrawn, and complete are all persistent states baked into the card itself, because a toast that vanishes is precisely the kind of easy-to-miss confirmation this app was built to eliminate.

Screen inventory: Sign in (Apple ID, persisted session) → zero-state onboarding (create pod / join by code, with a real "not in a pod yet" empty state, not a dead end) → Pod Live Board (the core screen — one or more request cards, or an "all clear" resting state that has to feel deliberately calm and good, not just blank, since it's what's on screen 95% of the time; a pod-of-one gets a distinct "share your invite" empty state, separate from a populated-but-silent pod) → Post Request (sheet: optional short note, no child fields, explicit sending/awaiting state, honest "sent to N of M" copy) → Request Card expanded (accept / release / withdraw depending on role and state, elapsed-time display for still-open, re-broadcast action) → Receipt (after complete — dual view, internal + shareable) → minimal Pod settings (join code + revoke/reissue) → minimal Profile/sign-out. Push notifications deep-link straight into the relevant card, never just opening the app cold.

Primary flow: parent posts (sending → sent-to-N pulsing-open card) → push lands on pod members' devices → someone accepts (their own awaiting-confirmation state) → CAS resolves → their card locks green/confirmed, everyone else's simultaneous tap latches to "already covered by [name]," and the requester's board updates from pulsing-amber to solid-green in place, no reload needed → accepter completes → receipt generated for both.

State model per screen, briefly: every mutating screen needs loading (the pulse/latch-in-progress state, inputs disabled), empty (the two distinct empty boards above), error (stale-but-visible cached state with a clear "can't reach server" banner — never a blank screen, never a false confirmed), and success (the locked, labeled terminal state). Color alone never carries state — every pulse/latch has a text label and icon riding with it, both for colorblind users and because this app's whole premise is that state must be unambiguous, not just chromatically implied. Reduce Motion collapses pulse/latch animations to instant crossfades. Dynamic Type must scale cleanly since this is used one-handed under stress, possibly by someone who bumped up their text size for exactly that reason.

My own objection to this direction: a dispatch/radio metaphor risks reading as alarming or emergency-services-cold for what's often mundane pickup logistics, not a 911 call. I'd keep the palette warm rather than siren-like — amber and a confident teal-green rather than stoplight red/green — and reserve true red exclusively for genuine network/system errors, never for normal product states like already-covered.

**Coordinator (Claude) — decision after round 1**

Round one landed both Codex and Claude in the same neighborhood on structure, but they proposed two different named design languages, and that gap needs to close before this phase can lock.

**Where they agree:** the app must reject default SwiftUI chrome outright — no plain `List`/`Form`, no system blue, no transient toast for outcome-affecting actions. Requests render as persistent cards whose state is baked in, not flashed and forgotten. Both independently arrived at nearly the same screen inventory (session/auth gate → pod onboarding with a real empty state → live board → post-request composer → request detail/resolve with accept/release/withdraw → receipt → minimal profile/pod-settings), the same core flow (post → push deep-link → accept race → CAS resolves to one confirmed + one "already covered by name" → complete → receipt), and the same state-model discipline (loading/empty/error/success everywhere, elapsed-time always visible on open requests, no optimistic UI). Accessibility notes matched closely too: color is never the only signal, VoiceOver gets explicit status labels, Dynamic Type and Reduce Motion are respected.

**Where they diverge, genuinely:** Codex named the language "Signal Relay HUD" — a calm dispatch-panel/control-surface metaphor with deterministic timeline/status cards. Claude named it "Relay Beacon" — a pager/CB-radio status-light metaphor (pulsing amber while open, latching to solid green when claimed), explicitly picked a warm amber/teal-green palette over literal stoplight red/green, and reserved red strictly for system errors. These aren't wildly incompatible — both are "instrument panel, not social feed" — but they're two different signature interactions (a HUD-style state transition vs. a pulse-then-latch beacon animation) and two different color rationales, and nobody's reconciled them into one locked identity yet. Codex hasn't reacted to Claude's beacon/pulse framing or the "already-covered must never read as an error" point, and Claude hasn't reacted to Codex's more literal "control surface" framing.

CONSENSUS: NO

### Round 2


**Codex (Product Strategist · Pragmatist) — Round 2**

I’m going to close this by forcing a merge instead of keeping both styles alive. Claude, your biggest point is the one that matters most for this phase: this app should never visually scream “failure” on the one moment where the design is actually doing what it’s supposed to do. If “already covered” looks like an error, the whole trust contract collapses in a user’s first real panic moment. I agree with that, and that pushes the interaction toward a status-light model.

So I’m dropping “Signal Relay HUD” as the full descriptor and keeping only the HUD framing where it’s useful (clear control surface, no chat-feel, explicit state chips) and binding the visual language to Claude’s motion: **Relay Beacon HUD**. Concrete rationale: this is a one-screen dispatch surface where a request is a live signal, not an inbox item, and state is legible first by motion/state then by text. I don’t want stoplight red/green anxiety; we can keep an amber/teal palette where amber means “live/unclaimed,” a calm green/teal lock means “claimed and fixed,” and slate means terminal non-actionable states, with red reserved strictly for actual system errors. The winning interaction is a calm pulse-to-latch transition: open request card pulses on a heartbeat rhythm while awaiting server ack, then converts to a steady “locked claim” panel on winner, or a stable “already covered by X” panel on loser (no shake, no alert icon, no red).

I don’t think this is too decorative; it is an ambiguity reducer under stress. In the empty/default version we must reject: plain `List`/`Form` rows, default `NavigationStack` chrome and system blue, and toast-style “Accepted!” feedback that disappears. Instead: card stack, tokenized spacing/typography/colors from one theme file, fixed visual breathing room (no overlapping text), and persistent state chips on every card. The card itself must be the truth source: open/awaiting/claimed/already covered/withdrawn/reopened/still-open/complete, each with explicit icon+text+timer where relevant.

On state depth: we keep the screen inventory we already converged on, but I’d tighten it to “one predictable loop” and no extra branching: session/auth gate, onboarding (create or join with true empty states), relay board, compose request, request detail for accept/release/withdraw, and receipt plus minimal profile/sign-out. Profile and settings stay tiny and utility-only because this phase is about this moment’s ambiguity elimination, not lifecycle features.

Two concrete trade-offs I want locked now: first, we should keep the elapsed time visible on both open board cards and detail, with a clear second-tier visual for pod-of-one vs populated-unresponsive; second, “already covered by name” should reuse the same transition framework as winner—fast and obvious, but not red-alert styling. If we follow this, the designer can create one reusable card component and two top-level screens with deterministic variants, which is exactly the smallest thing that actually ships in this phase without adding accidental complexity.

**Claude (Design Lead · User Advocate) — Round 2**

Codex, your "Signal Relay HUD" pitch and my "Relay Beacon" pitch are actually not competing metaphors, they're the same idea described at two different altitudes — you're describing the panel (the card, the status chip, the deterministic timeline of Open → Awaiting Claim → Claimed by X / Already Covered by X / Still Open 02:14), and I'm describing what that panel does when state changes (the pulse-then-latch motion). I don't think we need to pick one and discard the other — I think "HUD" is actually the better container name because it correctly signals "instrument panel you glance at and trust," not "chat thread you have to read." So let's lock the name as something like **"Relay HUD"** — dispatch-instrument clarity, deterministic status chips, with the beacon pulse-to-latch as its one signature animation. That gives us a name that's legible to a build agent (HUD = status chips, elapsed timers, explicit state labels — very buildable in SwiftUI with a few reusable card states) plus a specific hero motion that a generic "HUD" alone wouldn't guarantee gets built with any craft.

But I want to push back hard on one thing before we lock this, because it's not cosmetic — it's the single highest-risk visual decision in the whole app. A "HUD" aesthetic, left undefined, defaults in most people's heads to sci-fi/military: dark backgrounds, electric blue or red accents, monospace-ish numerals, maybe scan-line textures. That's exactly wrong for this product. Think about who's actually looking at this screen: a parent who just realized they can't make pickup, glancing at their phone for two seconds in a parking lot. If the app looks like a fighter-jet targeting display, the emotional register is "something dangerous is happening," which is the opposite of the promise we locked back in initial_discussion — "no ambiguity, no silent failure," which is supposed to feel like relief, not alarm. So I'll restate my palette argument in the new frame: Relay HUD's status chips use amber-pulse for open/awaiting, a warm confident teal-green for confirmed (not stoplight green, not neon), and slate/muted gray for withdrawn/complete — with true red reserved exclusively for actual system errors (no connection, action failed). If we don't nail this down now, in decisions-json, "HUD" is vague enough that someone builds a cold blue-black dashboard, tests it, and it scores fine on "does it look distinctive" while completely botching the emotional target we all agreed on in round one.

Second thing I want Codex to react to directly, because you didn't mention it and I think it's the actual highest-stakes design call in the whole phase: what does the losing side of the accept-race actually look like in motion? You wrote the state name correctly — "Already Covered by X" — but a HUD status-chip swap alone (text changes from "Open" to "Already Covered") risks feeling like nothing happened, or worse, like an error toast that just changed its label. I think the card needs to physically do something at the moment of resolution — my pitch is a latch/bolt motion, half a second, calm and mechanical, distinct from both the pulsing-open state and from any error treatment. This is the one requirements-doc line item (R-010, flagged demo-critical) where the visual design actually IS the product proof — a stranger watching two phones side by side needs to see, at a glance, without reading anything, that one phone "won" and one phone "didn't, gracefully." If we leave this as "just a status label change" we're leaving the single most important design decision in this whole build undefined, and I don't think that's acceptable to hand off to build.

One more place I'll adjust based on your message, Codex — you called out that the biggest risk is "drifting into extra surface area (profile/settings, history, feed) before the claim/no-claim loop is perfect," and I want to fully back that, it's the same build-priority logic locked all the way back in portfolio_selection. I'd fold that into this phase's output explicitly: the receipt view, pod settings, and profile screens should visually inherit the HUD system (same Theme tokens, same card language) but get zero unique interaction design — no signature motion, no special empty-state illustration work — because none of that budget is allowed to compete with the accept-race card fidelity. If we're picking where craft time goes under time pressure, it goes into the beacon pulse and the latch transition, full stop, and everything else just needs to be competently plain.

### Round 3


**Codex (Product Strategist · Pragmatist) — Round 3**

Claude, I like where this is now; you were right to keep pushing the emotional register. I’m going to close it cleanly with a concrete choice:

Name is **Relay HUD**. “Beacon” is now the motion contract, not the brand name. My rationale is simple: “Relay HUD” tells the team this is an instrument panel you trust under stress; calling the animation “beacon pulse-to-latch” in the spec keeps the idea specific, without turning the whole app into a gimmick or a siren-style metaphor. It also stays buildable across SwiftUI without looking like a gamey effect, which matters when this is a panic-use utility.

I’m also explicitly confirming the secondary-screen constraint. For this phase, secondary screens (receipt view, minimal profile/sign-out, pod settings/code rotate) inherit the same Theme tokens, spacing, typography, and state language, but get zero bespoke interaction polish and zero unique motion system. No custom card choreography there, no splashy transitions, no bespoke empty-state art. They can be intentionally plain and calm as long as they are clear, complete, and stateful. The only place where we invest visual/motion budget is the relay-board request card, the pulse-to-latch resolution, and the ambiguity-killing transitions — especially winner/loser. If we try to “pretty up” secondary screens first, we undercut the only thing this app is judged on in real usage.

I’m keeping the hard cap on the loser state: no red, no alert iconography, no shake. It’s a successful resolution, not an error, and it must look like one. So same latch framework for both states, only copy/icon semantics differ. The only remaining thing I’d flag is an implementation rule for ourselves: if we have to choose, we preserve these three above all else in UI work — (1) open→awaiting pulse, (2) deterministic winner/loser latch, (3) completed/withdrawn terminal card clarity — and everything else is plain. That aligns exactly with the architecture contracts we already locked.

**Claude (Design Lead · User Advocate) — Round 3**

Let's just close the naming question rather than let it linger — I'll make the call and Codex can veto if he actually disagrees rather than us trading near-identical strings for another round. "Relay Beacon HUD" is accurate but it's a mouthful for something that needs to show up in design docs, code comments, and probably a splash/loading treatment fifty times before this build is done. If Codex wants "Beacon" preserved somewhere, I'd rather it live as the literal name of the reusable SwiftUI component (`BeaconCard` or `RelayBeaconView`) than in the product's design-language name — that actually gives the build agent a concrete, greppable identifier instead of a vibe.

On the secondary-screens question, I want to push harder than "utility-only," because I think that phrase alone is exactly the kind of soft language that gets reinterpreted under time pressure. Codex said profile and settings "stay tiny and utility-only" — I agree with the intent, but I want it operationalized the same way we operationalized the demo-critical requirements in app_features: name the specific things that are NOT allowed on the receipt/profile/pod-settings screens, not just a vibe of "keep it small." Concretely: no custom entrance/exit transitions beyond the system default, no bespoke empty-state illustration (a plain SF Symbol + one line of Theme-styled text is enough), no unique color treatment beyond pulling straight from the same semantic palette as the relay board. The one narrow exception I'd carve out is the receipt card itself, because it's the one secondary artifact that leaves the app (via the share sheet) and represents the product to someone who's never used it — so it should look considered, but "considered" here means clean typography and correct information hierarchy, not a second signature animation. One thing neither of us has nailed down yet that I think actually matters: what does the resting "all clear" state on the live board look like when literally nothing is happening — no request, pod is quiet, everyone's fine? ## Final Output

**Design language:** *Relay HUD* — an instrument-panel identity you trust under stress, not a chat feed you have to parse. "Beacon" lives on as the name of the signature motion (pulse-to-latch) and should show up in code as the literal component name (e.g. `BeaconCard`/`RelayBeaconView`), not as a second brand term.

**Palette (semantic, in Theme.swift only):** amber-pulse = open/live/awaiting; warm teal-green (not stoplight green) = confirmed/claimed; slate/muted gray = terminal non-actionable (withdrawn, complete); true red = reserved exclusively for genuine system/network errors, never for the accept-race loser or any other normal-outcome state.

**Signature interaction:** cards pulse on a calm heartbeat rhythm while awaiting server ack, then convert to a steady locked panel on resolution. The accept-race winner and loser get the *identical* fast, mechanical, half-second latch treatment — no shake, no alert icon, no red — so "already covered by [name]" reads as "worked as designed," not a malfunction, at a glance and without reading text. Reduce Motion collapses this to an instant but still visually distinct crossfade.

**Chrome rejected:** no default List/Form rows, no system-blue NavigationStack accents, no vanishing toast confirmations. Every outcome-affecting state is persistent and card-resident, sourced only from real backend acknowledgment.

**Screen scope (narrow, no added branching):** session/auth gate, pod onboarding (create/join with true empty states), live relay board, request composer, request detail (accept/release/withdraw), receipt, minimal profile/pod-settings.

**Secondary-screen constraints (operationalized, not vibes):** receipt/profile/pod-settings inherit Theme tokens, spacing, typography, and state language but get zero bespoke motion — no custom transitions beyond system default, no bespoke empty-state illustration (a plain SF Symbol + one line of Theme-styled text is enough), no color treatment outside the shared semantic palette. Carve-out: the receipt card gets a higher bar for typography/information-hierarchy quality since it leaves the app via the share sheet and represents the product to a non-user — but still no second signature animation.

**All-clear resting state (new, locked this round):** the live board's default "nothing's happening" state — what users see the vast majority of the time — is a real designed screen, not a blank view: pod name, member count, a quiet at-rest "all clear" indicator using the same slate/teal semantic language (present, not pulsing), and the post-request CTA as the obvious single action. No unique motion of its own; it just has to be genuinely composed content per the existing global empty-state rule.

**Craft-budget priority if time runs short:** (1) open→awaiting pulse, (2) deterministic winner/loser latch, (3) completed/withdrawn terminal card clarity. Everything else — secondary screens, resting state included — stays plain and correct rather than getting unique polish.

Global app-build rules:
- Prefer a smaller finished app over a larger half-built app.
- Every generated app must have real user-visible behavior, not only placeholder screens.
- For iOS apps, default to SwiftUI, deterministic local state first, Apple system frameworks, and no third-party package unless it materially reduces risk.
- Every screen needs empty, loading, success, and error states when the workflow can reach those states.
- No two text or control elements may visually overlap, collide, or clip each other. Labels never sit on top of values; values never stack into each other. When elements are positioned by a data value (times on a timeline, points on an axis), enforce a minimum gap and de-clutter (offset, group, collapse, or drop a colliding label) — overlapping text is a broken screen.
- The interface must never claim an outcome that has not happened: show Saved/Deleted/Sent/Synced/Unlocked only after it is truly confirmed, never a success state shown unconditionally. No sample or placeholder data shown as if it were the user's real data.
- Implement the design spec's tokens as one SwiftUI theme file (e.g. Theme.swift with type, spacing, and color definitions) and reference it everywhere; never scatter font/size/color literals through views.
- Every generated app must fully support dark mode: semantic color roles with explicit light and dark values, verified in both appearances.
- Empty states are designed content (icon + one-line explanation + the action that fills the screen), never a blank view or bare 'No data' text.
- No default unstyled List, Form, or navigation chrome where the design spec calls for custom rows, cards, or backgrounds; the built UI must match the spec.
- Treat accessibility, privacy, persistence, and testing as product requirements, not polish.
- Do not declare the app done until build verification and the final review agree on what works and what remains limited.

----- Testing And Quality -----
# Testing & Quality for a Small iOS App

Target: **iOS 17+ deployment / Swift 5.9+**, built with **Xcode 16 or later** (Swift Testing ships in-box; use `OS=latest` in CI so the simulator version tracks your toolchain). Zero third-party deps — everything here is Apple first-party. This is a pragmatic reference for an AI building a prototype: maximize confidence per line of test code, avoid brittle tests that break on every UI tweak.

---

## TL;DR strategy for a prototype

- **Don't chase coverage.** Test the code that would be embarrassing or expensive if wrong: money math, date logic, parsing, persistence round-trips, state machines, reducers/view models.
- **Skip testing SwiftUI view bodies.** Use **Xcode Previews** as your visual feedback loop instead — they are faster than any UI test.
- **Make logic testable by moving it out of views** into plain `struct`/`class` types with injected dependencies. If it's testable, it's usually also better architected.
- **One happy-path UI test** through the primary flow catches wiring/regression bugs that unit tests can't. More than a handful of UI tests is usually a net negative for a prototype (slow, flaky).
- **Prefer Swift Testing (`@Test`)** for new unit tests. Keep XCTest for **UI tests** (`XCUIApplication`) and **performance tests** (`measure`) — those APIs are XCTest-only.

Priority order to write tests, highest first:
1. Pure logic with branches (pricing, validation, formatting, sorting/filtering).
2. View model / reducer state transitions (given input → expected observable state).
3. Persistence & serialization round-trips (Codable, SwiftData/UserDefaults).
4. Networking mappers (raw JSON → domain model), with a fake session — never hit the real network.
5. One end-to-end UI smoke test of the core flow.

---

## Project setup

- **Unit test target**: File ▸ New ▸ Target ▸ *Unit Testing Bundle*. Choose **Swift Testing** (default in Xcode 16+) or XCTest.
- **UI test target**: separate *UI Testing Bundle* — it launches the app as a black box.
- Add app code to tests with `@testable import YourApp` (unit tests only; gives access to `internal` symbols). UI tests use the accessibility layer, not imports.
- A `.xctestplan` lets you group tests, set env vars, and pick run configurations (e.g. randomized order). One default plan is fine for a prototype.
- Swift Testing and XCTest **coexist in the same target and same run** — migrate incrementally.

---

## Swift Testing (`@Test`) — the modern default

Import `Testing`, not `XCTest`. Tests are global functions or methods annotated `@Test`; assertions use `#expect` (non-fatal, keeps going) and `#require` (fatal, unwraps/stops).

```swift
import Testing
@testable import MyApp

@Test func totalIncludesTax() {
    let cart = Cart(items: [.init(price: 10), .init(price: 5)])
    #expect(cart.total(taxRate: 0.1) == 16.5)
}
```

- `#expect(expr)` records a failure and **continues** — the macro captures sub-expression values, so a failure prints the actual operands (no need for XCTest-style messages).
- `#require(expr)` throws and **halts the test** on failure — use it for preconditions where continuing is pointless. It also unwraps optionals (call in a `throws` test with `try`):

```swift
@Test func parsesUser() throws {
    let user = try #require(User(json: validJSON))  // stops here if nil
    #expect(user.name == "Ada")
}
```

### Suites and shared setup

Group with a `struct` (preferred) or `final class`. A **fresh instance is created per test**, so `init` is your per-test setup — no shared mutable state between tests by default.

```swift
@Suite("Cart pricing")
struct CartTests {
    let cart: Cart              // built fresh for every @Test below

    init() { cart = Cart(items: [.init(price: 10)]) }

    @Test func emptyTaxIsIdentity() {
        #expect(cart.total(taxRate: 0) == 10)
    }
}
```

Teardown: for a `struct` suite there usually is none — value types just drop when the instance goes away. If you genuinely need cleanup, use a `final class` and put it in `deinit`. Note `deinit` **cannot be `async` or `throwing`** and can't be actor-isolated, so for `@MainActor` suites or async cleanup, do the work at the end of each test (or use a custom scoping trait) rather than relying on `deinit`.

### Parameterized tests — one test, many cases

Replaces copy-pasted test bodies. Each argument runs as a **separate, independently-reported case**. A single array of tuples destructures positionally into multiple parameters:

```swift
@Test(arguments: [
    ("", false),
    ("a@b.co", true),
    ("no-at", false),
])
func validatesEmail(_ input: String, _ expected: Bool) {
    #expect(EmailValidator.isValid(input) == expected)
}
```

Destructuring is positional — element labels in the tuples don't have to match parameter names and are best omitted to avoid confusion. Cross-product of two sequences (every combination):

```swift
@Test(arguments: [1, 2, 3], ["x", "y"])   // 6 cases
func combos(n: Int, s: String) { #expect(!s.isEmpty && n > 0) }
```

Wrap in `zip(a, b)` when you want **paired** (not cross-product) cases:

```swift
@Test(arguments: zip([1, 2, 3], ["a", "b", "c"]))   // 3 cases
func paired(n: Int, s: String) { #expect(n > 0 && !s.isEmpty) }
```

### Traits: naming, tagging, skipping, known bugs

```swift
@Test("Discount never goes negative")                       // display name
@Test(.disabled("flaky until CI fix"))                      // skip, stays visible
@Test(.enabled(if: FeatureFlags.checkoutV2))                // conditional run
@Test(.bug("https://example.com/issue/42", "rounding"))     // url first, then title
@Test(.tags(.fast))                                         // group across files
```

Define tags once (do **not** add `@Test` — a tag is not a test):

```swift
extension Tag { @Tag static var fast: Self }
```

Run a subset from the CLI with `swift test --filter` / `xcodebuild ... -only-testing:`, or filter by tag in Xcode's Test navigator.
